young.html: Anton Chekhov was a Russian doctor who also wrote stories and plays. He liked to show ordinary people as they really are: a little funny, a little sad, and always hoping for something better.

In Uncle Vanya, Vanya and his niece Sonya have worked for years on a country farm. They send all the money it earns to Sonya's father, a famous professor in the city, because they think his work is important. Then the professor comes to live with them, and they discover he is not as great as they believed. At the end, Sonya says they must keep going, keep working, and be kind to others, and one day they will rest.

young.html: Plant a tree. The country doctor in the play, Astrov, plants young trees because forests take a hundred years to grow. With a grown-up, plant a seed or a seedling, and make a label: who planted it, the date, and who might sit in its shade someday.

full.html: Anton Chekhov (1860–1904) grew up in Taganrog in southern Russia, the grandson of a serf. He trained as a doctor in Moscow and paid his way by writing comic sketches, then became one of the great masters of the short story. His four late plays, The Seagull, Uncle Vanya, Three Sisters and The Cherry Orchard, changed the theater. Uncle Vanya was published in 1897 and staged by the Moscow Art Theatre in 1899. Its subtitle is "Scenes from Country Life."

Vanya and his niece Sonya have run the family estate for twenty-five years, sending its income to Sonya's father, Professor Serebryakov, whose writings they once worshipped. Now the retired professor has come to stay with his beautiful young second wife, Yelena, and the household falls apart. Vanya decides the professor is a fraud and that he has wasted his life. Both Vanya and the country doctor, Astrov, are drawn to Yelena. Sonya quietly loves Astrov, who hardly notices her.
Astrov is one of Chekhov's most modern figures. He plants forests and makes maps showing how the district's woods are disappearing. Sonya repeats his ideas:

full.text: He says that forests are the ornaments of the earth, that they teach mankind to understand beauty and attune his mind to lofty sentiments.
full.author: Chekhov
full.ed: Plays by Anton Tchekoff (Charles Scribner's Sons, New York)
full.note: Fell spells the names Sonia and Astroff.

full.html: In Act III the professor announces a plan to sell the estate, which would leave Vanya and Sonya with nothing. Vanya explodes, and in a rage fires a pistol at him twice, missing both times. In Act IV the guests leave, Astrov drives off, and Vanya and Sonya sit down to the account books again. Sonya speaks the play's last words:

full.text: What can we do? We must live our lives. Yes, we shall live, Uncle Vanya.
full.author: Chekhov
full.ed: Plays by Anton Tchekoff (Charles Scribner's Sons, New York)

full.html: She goes on to say that they will work for others, bear their trials patiently, and after death find rest and peace with God: "I have faith, Uncle, fervent, passionate faith."

full.html: Chekhov's drama happens under the surface. People talk about the weather, tea and the harvest while their lives are quietly breaking. Nothing much "happens," and yet everything changes for Vanya and Sonya.
Calling the play simply gloomy. Chekhov thought of his plays as partly comic, and the characters' self-pity is often funny. Sonya's ending is sad, but it is also about endurance, work and hope.

items: Ibsen, in the 19th-century rungs, put hidden truths on stage in a living room; Chekhov goes further, keeping the big moments almost offstage.
Tolstoy, whom Chekhov admired, asked how one should live; Chekhov asks the same question without giving a sermon.
Beckett's Waiting for Godot, at the end of this ladder, also shows people waiting and talking while time passes.
Chekhov's habit of letting a play end quietly, with no grand speech of resolution, shaped much of 20th-century drama and the modern short story.
Was Vanya's life wasted, as he says? What would make a life of quiet work worthwhile?
Is it good to admire someone so much that you work for them for years?
Why does Astrov plant forests he will never see grown?
What gives Sonya the strength to go on?

questions: Vanya worked for years for someone he admired. What happens when we find out a hero is ordinary?
Why do you think Sonya does not tell Astrov how she feels until it is too late?
Astrov plants forests for people a hundred years from now. Who will enjoy something you do today?
Is the ending of the play sad, hopeful, or both?
Chekhov said a play should show life as it is. What everyday moment in your family would make a good scene?
